messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Harold, a 76-year-old divorced man who had managed the same midtown hotel for nearly four decades, could still summon the smell of it. Not the image—that remained fractured, a slide deck of disconnected moments: the housekeeper’s panicked knock, the acrid yellow haze seeping under the maintenance door, the chemical burn at the back of his throat. But the smell came whole and unbidden, a metallic sweetness that flooded his chest with terror before his mind could even register what was happening. He had been supervising a routine pipe repair in the basement when a corroded valve burst, releasing a cloud of industrial solvent into the sealed room. He got everyone out, but not before he had inhaled deeply. In the weeks that followed, he could not trust his own body. It kept reacting as if he were still in that basement—heart hammering, skin prickling, breath short—even when he was standing in his quiet kitchen. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his ally, that it would betray him at any moment, and that he was fundamentally helpless to stop bad things from happening.

The helplessness bled into everything. Harold began to feel that the world was shot through with hidden threats, and he found himself scanning his environment constantly. At home—the only place that felt even remotely safe—he was still on guard, flinching at the rumble of the garbage truck or the sudden slam of a neighbor’s door. He had reduced his safe places to three: his apartment, the small park bench by the river where he could see all approaches, and the hotel lobby during the quiet morning shift. Everywhere else felt like a potential trap. The sense of threat was so pervasive that it began to feed back into his memories; the more vigilant he became, the more often the disconnected fragments of that day intruded, often triggered by nothing more than an unexpected sound. A dropped pan in the hotel kitchen could send him right back to the hiss of the ruptured valve, his throat closing, the metallic smell ghosting through his sinuses even though nothing was there.

To manage the intrusions, Harold had developed a set of strategies that made sense to him but that he knew, in quieter moments, were not really working. He kept the television or a radio playing loudly at all times in his apartment, drowning out the silence that his mind would otherwise fill with the sound of that hissing pipe. He also monitored his own thoughts constantly, scanning for any sign that he was losing control, that the terror might break through and he would finally go crazy. The effort was exhausting, and it only reinforced his sense that his body was unreliable—that he had to police himself because he could not trust his own mind. He had also stopped going anywhere near the hotel basement, taking the long way around the building to reach the main office, and he had instructed his assistant to handle any maintenance issues personally. This avoidance had begun to strain his working relationships; his staff noticed he was jumpy, less available, and he had started delegating tasks he had once prided himself on handling directly.

The cycle tightened. The more he avoided and monitored, the more convinced he became that he could not cope, that his helplessness was a permanent fact. And the more helpless he felt, the more on guard he became, scanning for danger even in the safety of his own home. His sleep was poor, his appetite diminished, and he had lost touch with most of his friends, who had grown tired of his refusal to go to restaurants or social gatherings. What finally brought Harold to seek help was a moment in the hotel lobby last Tuesday, when a delivery driver dropped a metal dolly on the marble floor. The crack sent Harold into a full panic attack in front of the front desk staff. He could not breathe, could not speak, and for several minutes he was certain he was dying. Afterward, he sat in his office with the door locked, trembling, and realized that he could not keep living this way. He was most afraid that the therapy would fail, that he would be told he was too old to change, and that the rest of his life would be spent trapped in that basement, over and over.
